albums.blurb: Composed with producer Daniel Lanois and Eno's brother Roger for Al Reinert's documentary about the Apollo missions (eventually released as For All Mankind), this 1983 record sits at the melodic end of Eno's ambient run after Music for Airports and On Land. It is entirely instrumental, and its second half, led by Lanois's pedal steel, plays like country music in zero gravity. The Spotify link is the 2019 Extended Edition, which appends an instrumental companion disc the trio's survivors recorded for the mission's 50th anniversary.
albums.reception: AllMusic's review calls it "easily one of Eno's best and most accessible ambient albums" and an ideal starting point for anyone new to the genre.

albums.album: How to Live with a Phantom
albums.blurb: Sakamoto spent two decades fronting the Tokyo psych-rock institution Yura Yura Teikoku before dissolving the band and re-emerging with this solo debut, the first release on his own zelone records. He wrote everything and played nearly every note himself, trading his old band's noise for laid-back, softly grooving funk and soft rock with touches of exotica and city pop, sung in a deadpan murmur.
albums.reception: Its 2012 international release through New York's Other Music Recording Co. drew coverage from SPIN and Stereophile, with critics comparing its mellow one-man grooves to Todd Rundgren.

albums.blurb: The Rio singer-guitarist Joyce (billed today as Joyce Moreno) had been recording since 1968, but this 1980 EMI album of entirely her own compositions, arranged with Maurício Maestro and played by a first-call cast of Brazilian musicians, is the centerpiece of her catalogue. Its songs, including the title track and "Clareana," took the experience of womanhood and motherhood as their explicit subject, which was still rare in Brazilian popular song.
albums.reception: Joyce reached the finals of the Festival MPB-80 competition with "Clareana," which became her first chart success in Brazil and carried the album to samba-classic status.
